Polyfill Promise.any

Promise.any is the mirror image of Promise.all: it resolves with the first fulfilled value and rejects only if every promise rejects, with an AggregateError holding all reasons in input order. Compare: race settles with the first to settle (fulfilled or rejected), and allSettled never rejects. Use case: query several mirrors and take whichever answers first.
Implement a minimal Promise (then chaining, catch, async resolution)

The essentials: three states and a value; settle only once; store callbacks while pending; then returns a new promise resolved with the callback's return value (or rejected if it throws); callbacks always run asynchronously as microtasks; and a returned promise is adopted, which is what makes chaining flatten. The full Promises/A+ spec adds a few more edge cases (such as rejecting when a promise resolves to itself).
setInterval using setTimeout, with a way to stop it

Recursive setTimeout guarantees a gap of delay between the end of one run and the start of the next, while setInterval fires on a fixed schedule and can pile up calls if the callback (or an async request it starts) takes longer than the interval. That's why polling code often uses this pattern. Timers are minimum delays, not exact: they wait for the call stack and earlier tasks.
Render a template string: "Hello {{name}}, you have {{count}} messages"

String.prototype.replace with a global regex and a callback is the key tool: the callback receives the whole match and each capture group. If the output goes into HTML, escape the values (&, <, >, quotes) to prevent XSS; frameworks like Angular do this for you in interpolation. O(n) in the template length.
Convert between camelCase, snake_case, kebab-case and Title Case

Normalise every format into a list of lower-case words first, then join them in the target style; this keeps each converter to one line. A common real use is mapping snake_case JSON from a backend (for example PHP or Python) to camelCase objects in the front end.
Shuffle an array fairly (Fisher–Yates) and pick a random element

Fisher–Yates gives every permutation an equal chance in O(n) time. The popular sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5) trick is biased, because sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, and it costs O(n log n). For anything security-related (tokens, OTPs) use crypto.getRandomValues or crypto.randomUUID() instead of Math.random.
